tips.title: Open for strict, filled for or equal to
tips.body: $<$ and $>$ get an **open** circle, because the endpoint is not a solution. $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ get a **filled** one, because it is. The circle is worth its own mark, so decide it from the symbol before you draw anything.

tips.title: Dividing by a negative reverses the symbol
tips.body: It is the only step in solving an inequality that differs from solving an equation. $2 < 5$, but $-2 > -5$: multiplying by a negative reflects the number line and swaps which is bigger, so the symbol must swap too.

tips.title: Move x to the side where it is positive
tips.body: For $5 - 2x \geqslant 1$, add $2x$ instead of dividing by $-2$: $5 \geqslant 1 + 2x$, then $4 \geqslant 2x$, then $2 \geqslant x$. The x term stays positive throughout, so the flip you might forget never comes up.

tips.title: Test each end against its own symbol
tips.body: For integer solutions of $-2 \leqslant x < 3$, check the ends separately: $-2$ is **in** because of $\leqslant$, 3 is **out** because of $<$. And count the negatives — starting at zero loses $-2$ and $-1$.

why.matters:
An equation says a quantity is one number. An inequality says it is somewhere in a range — and **almost every real specification is a range**, because nothing can be made, measured or delivered to an exact value.

So the number line is not a teaching device that gets put away later. It is the honest picture of what a requirement actually is: a stretch of values that pass, with an end that is either included or not, and that distinction decides real things.

examples.title: Nothing is made to exactly the right size
examples.body:
A drawing calls for a shaft 50 mm across. No machine can produce exactly 50, and no gauge could prove it had. So the drawing does not ask for it. It asks for 50 mm with a tolerance of $\pm0.05$, which means $49.95 \leqslant d \leqslant 50.05$.

That is the whole specification, and it is an inequality on a number line: two ends, both included, and everything between them passes. The permitted band is 0.1 mm wide — about the thickness of a sheet of paper.

The closed circles matter here in a way they never seem to in a textbook. A shaft measuring exactly 50.05 passes; one measuring a hair over is scrap. Somebody decided which, and wrote it with the symbol that says so.

steps.title: Reading the four symbols
steps.body:
An **inequality** says one thing is bigger or smaller than another, rather than equal to it. Four symbols do all the work.

- $x < 5$ — x is **less than** 5. Five itself is **not** included.
- $x > 5$ — x is **greater than** 5.
- $x \leqslant 5$ — x is **less than or equal to** 5. Five **is** included.
- $x \geqslant 5$ — x is **greater than or equal to** 5.

The line underneath is the whole difference: it means *or equal to*, and it decides whether the endpoint counts.

A good way to keep the direction straight: the symbol **opens towards the larger side**. In $x < 5$ the wide end faces the 5, so 5 is the larger. In $7 > 2$ the wide end faces the 7.

An inequality usually has **infinitely many** solutions, not one. $x < 5$ is satisfied by 4, by 4.9, by $-100$, and by every number below 5. That is why we draw the answer rather than writing a single number.

steps.title: Showing it on a number line
steps.body:
A solution set is drawn on a number line with a **circle** at the boundary and a **line** over the numbers that work.

- **Open circle** for $<$ or $>$: the endpoint is **not** included.
- **Filled circle** for $\leqslant$ or $\geqslant$: the endpoint **is** included.

Then shade towards the numbers that satisfy it, with an **arrow** if the solution carries on forever.

That is the whole convention, and it is worth being precise about, because an open circle where a filled one belongs loses the mark even when the algebra is perfect.

A quick way to check your drawing: pick a number in the shaded part and test it in the original inequality. If it works, you have shaded the right side.

steps.title: Solving one
steps.body:
Solving an inequality works **exactly like solving an equation**: do the same thing to both sides until $x$ is alone.

There is one difference, and it is the thing this topic is really testing. **If you multiply or divide by a negative number, the symbol reverses.**

Why? Because $2 < 5$, but multiplying both sides by $-1$ gives $-2$ and $-5$ — and $-2$ is **greater** than $-5$. The order has flipped, so the symbol must flip with it.

steps.title: Double inequalities
steps.body:
Sometimes $x$ is trapped between two numbers:

$$-3 \leqslant 2x + 1 < 7$$

This is really two inequalities at once. Solve it by doing the same thing to **all three parts**.

1. Subtract 1 everywhere: $-4 \leqslant 2x < 6$
2. Divide everything by 2: $-2 \leqslant x < 3$

So $x$ is between $-2$ and $3$, **including** $-2$ but **not** 3. On a number line that is a **filled** circle at $-2$, an **open** circle at 3, and shading between them. No arrows, because the solution does not carry on.

If a step involves dividing by a negative, the symbols reverse **and** the whole inequality is usually rewritten the other way round, so the smaller number is on the left. Keeping the smaller number on the left is what makes a double inequality readable.

steps.title: Integer solutions
steps.body:
A very common question asks for the **integer** solutions: the whole numbers that satisfy the inequality.

For $-2 \leqslant x < 3$ the integers are

$$-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$$

That is 5 values. Two things decide the ends, and both are easy to get wrong.

- $-2$ **is** included, because the symbol is $\leqslant$.
- $3$ is **not** included, because the symbol is $<$.

So check each end separately against its own symbol. Writing the solution set on a number line first makes this almost automatic: the filled circle is in, the open circle is out.

Watch for negative numbers. Students often start counting at 0 and forget that $-2$ and $-1$ are integers too.

check.solution: The integers are $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$: **5** of them. $-2$ is in because of $\leqslant$; 3 is out because of $<$.

steps.title: Higher tier: set notation, and why the symbol flips
steps.body:
**Set notation** is the Higher tier addition to this topic. The solution $x > 2$ is written

$$\{x : x > 2\}$$

which reads *the set of values of x such that x is greater than 2*. The colon means **such that**.

A double inequality goes inside one pair of brackets:

$$\{x : -2 \leqslant x < 3\}$$

And two separate pieces are joined with $\cup$, the union:

$$\{x : x < -1\} \cup \{x : x > 4\}$$

which is how you write *x is less than $-1$ or greater than 4* — two rays with a gap between them.

**Why dividing by a negative reverses the symbol.** It is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it is the step examiners target.

Start with something obviously true: $2 < 5$. Multiply both sides by $-1$: the numbers become $-2$ and $-5$. On a number line $-2$ is to the **right** of $-5$, so $-2 > -5$. Multiplying by a negative **reflects** the number line, and reflecting swaps which number is bigger. So the symbol must swap too.

A safer route if you find the flip error-prone: **move the x term to the side where it is positive** instead. For $5 - 2x \geqslant 1$, add $2x$ to both sides to get $5 \geqslant 1 + 2x$, then $4 \geqslant 2x$, then $2 \geqslant x$ — which is $x \leqslant 2$. Same answer, no flip needed at any point.

That trick is worth having, because it removes the single commonest error in the topic.

check.prompt: Which is the correct set notation for $-2 \leqslant x < 3$?
check.solution: Set notation needs the **curly brackets** and the colon meaning *such that*: $\{x : -2 \leqslant x < 3\}$. $\{-2, 3\}$ would be a set of just two numbers.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- $<$ and $>$ **exclude** the endpoint; $\leqslant$ and $\geqslant$ **include** it.
- On a number line: **open circle** for strict, **filled circle** for or equal to. Shade towards the numbers that work, with an **arrow** if it carries on.
- Solve an inequality exactly like an equation, with one exception.
- **Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the symbol.**
- Avoid the flip entirely by moving the x term to the side where it is **positive**.
- For a double inequality, do the same thing to **all three parts**.
- For integer solutions, test **each end against its own symbol**, and do not forget the negative integers.
- $-2 \leqslant x < 3$ has the integer solutions $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$.
- **Higher tier**: set notation is $\{x : x > 2\}$, where the colon means *such that*.
- Two separate pieces join with $\cup$: $\{x : x < -1\} \cup \{x : x > 4\}$.
- Always check by substituting a number that should work and one that should not.

questions.solution: Start by subtracting one from all three parts, which gives minus six is less than three x, which is less than or equal to nine. Then divide all three parts by three, which gives minus two is less than x, which is less than or equal to three. Since three is positive, no symbol reverses. On a number line this is an open circle at minus two, because the symbol there is strictly less than, and a filled circle at three, because that end includes the value, with the line shaded between them and no arrows. The integer solutions are minus one, zero, one, two and three. Minus two is excluded because the circle there is open, while three is included because its circle is filled, so there are five integer solutions in total.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Solving.** Subtract 1 from all three parts:

$$-6 < 3x \leqslant 9$$

Divide all three by 3. Three is positive, so nothing reverses:

$$-2 < x \leqslant 3$$

**On the number line.** An **open** circle at $-2$, because that end is strict. A **filled** circle at 3, because that end includes the value. Shade **between** them, with **no arrows** — the solution does not carry on.

**Integer solutions.** $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ — five of them. $-2$ is out because its circle is open; 3 is in because its circle is filled.

Testing each end against **its own** symbol is what makes this reliable.

questions.prompt: A student solves $4 - 2x > 10$ and writes $x > -3$. Explain the mistake and give the correct solution.
questions.solution: The student has subtracted four from both sides correctly, giving minus two x is greater than six, and has then divided both sides by minus two to reach the value minus three. The mistake is that they have kept the symbol pointing the same way. Dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the symbol, because multiplying by a negative reflects the number line and so swaps which of the two numbers is larger. The correct solution is therefore x is less than minus three, not greater than it. This can be checked by substituting a value. Taking x equal to minus four gives four minus two times minus four, which is four plus eight, or twelve, and twelve is indeed greater than ten, so minus four is a solution. Since minus four is less than minus three, the correct inequality must be x is less than minus three.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The mistake.** The student reached $-2x > 6$ correctly, then divided by $-2$ **without reversing the symbol**.

**Why it reverses.** Multiplying or dividing by a negative **reflects** the number line, which swaps which of two numbers is larger. $2 < 5$, but $-2 > -5$.

**The correct solution.**

$$4 - 2x > 10 \;\Rightarrow\; -2x > 6 \;\Rightarrow\; x < -3$$

**The check.** Take $x = -4$: $4 - 2(-4) = 4 + 8 = 12$, and $12 > 10$ ✓. Since $-4$ **is** a solution and $-4 < -3$, the answer must be $x < -3$, not $x > -3$.

Substituting one value would have caught this in a few seconds.

examTechnique.body:
Solve exactly as you would an equation, and watch for one step only: multiplying or dividing by a negative. If that is coming, consider moving the x term to the other side instead so it never happens.

Always substitute at the end. Put in a number that should work and one that should not. It takes seconds and it catches a reversed symbol immediately.

When you draw the solution, decide each circle from its own symbol before drawing, and add an arrow only if the solution carries on.

For integer solutions, test both ends separately, and remember that negative integers count.

At Higher tier, use curly brackets and the colon for set notation, and the union symbol for two separate pieces.

If the question says *show your answer on a number line*, the diagram is worth marks in itself: circles of the right kind, shading the right way, and an arrow where one belongs.
examinerErrors: Forgetting to reverse the symbol when dividing by a negative.
Drawing an open circle where the symbol includes the endpoint.
Shading the wrong side of the circle.
Leaving an arrow on a bounded solution, or omitting one from a solution that continues.
Listing integer solutions but starting at zero and missing the negative ones.
Including the endpoint in a list of integer solutions when the symbol is strict.
Changing only part of a double inequality instead of all three parts.
Writing set notation without the curly brackets or without the colon.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer avoids the negative division altogether by rearranging so the x term is positive, and then substitutes a value to confirm the direction rather than trusting the algebra. It reads each circle off its own symbol, so a double inequality gets one open and one filled circle without hesitation. Asked for integer solutions, it tests the two ends separately and counts the negatives. And when a mistake is presented to it, it explains the reflection of the number line rather than restating the rule.
